stories.title: Greece's Most Famous Oracle Sat Above A Gas Vent
stories.description: For over a thousand years kings consulted a priestess who prophesied in a trance at Delphi, and ancient writers blamed vapours from the rock. Geologists found the faults and named the gas. #history #unsolvedmysteries #ancientgreece
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's top hook cohort states a physical fact that reframes a familiar subject (Bloop, 133.1%), so this hook puts the temple on top of leaking faults in the first line instead of easing in through Delphi's fame.

hook_candidates.text: The oracle's temple sat on two faults leaking sweet gas
hook_candidates.why: Reframes a famous subject with a physical fact in one line.

hook_candidates.text: A priestess prophesied for a thousand years above a crack
hook_candidates.why: Atmospheric but vaguer, and 'crack' undersells it.

hook_candidates.text: Ancient writers said vapours rose under her. They were right
hook_candidates.why: Needs a referent for 'her' before it lands.

hook_choice.reason: It puts the geology and the prophecy in the same breath, which is the whole story, and needs no knowledge of Delphi to sound wrong.

factual_claims.text: The Temple of Apollo at Delphi in central Greece housed the oracle from at least the 8th century BC until about AD 390.
The Pythia delivered prophecies from a gilded tripod in the temple's inner sanctum, the adyton, while in a trance state, with priests recasting her words into verse.
Ancient sources, particularly Plutarch, described intoxicating vapours rising from an underground fissure beneath the temple floor.

In the 1980s geologist Jelle Zeilinga de Boer, archaeologist John Hale, chemist Jeffrey Chanton and toxicologist Henry Spiller found that the Kerna and Delphic fault lines cross directly below where the adyton stood.

The team proposed ethylene, a sweet-smelling gas from bituminous limestone that produces euphoria in small doses, while critics including Daryn Lehoux have disputed whether the concentrations were sufficient.

segments.narration: The oracle's temple sat on two faults leaking sweet gas. Delphi, central Greece. Kings and generals came here for over a thousand years.
The Pythia sat on a gilded tripod in the inner sanctum, the adyton. She went into a trance. Priests recast what came out as verse.
Plutarch wrote that intoxicating vapours rose from a fissure under the floor. For centuries that was filed away as temple myth. It was not.
In the 1980s a geologist, an archaeologist, a chemist and a toxicologist mapped the site. Two fault lines, Kerna and Delphic, cross directly beneath the sanctum.
Below them: bituminous limestone. The gas is ethylene — sweet-smelling, and in small doses euphoric. Critics still argue the dose. The faults are not in doubt.

research.summary: The Delphic oracle operated at the Temple of Apollo from at least the 8th century BC until c.AD 390. A four-year interdisciplinary study by de Boer (geology), Hale (archaeology), Chanton (chemistry) and Spiller (toxicology) identified the Kerna and Delphic faults crossing beneath the adyton over bituminous limestone, and found ethane, methane and ethylene in nearby spring water (ethylene at 0.3 ppm today, likely higher in antiquity). Ethylene causes euphoria and a floating sensation in small doses. The hypothesis is contested — Daryn Lehoux argued it is impossible, and methane and CO2/H2S have been proposed instead — so the narration states the faults as established and the dose as disputed.

stories.title: He Filmed The First Movie, Then Vanished From A Train
stories.description: Louis Le Prince shot moving pictures in Leeds in 1888, years before Edison's public claim. In 1890 he boarded a train at Dijon and was never seen again — no body, no luggage. #unsolvedmysteries #history #cinema
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strongest hooks state a vanishing plainly and specifically (Flight 19, 112.1%, 'fourteen men walked into the Florida sky and never returned'), so this hook pairs the achievement and the disappearance in one line before any name or date.

hook_candidates.text: He shot the first moving picture, then vanished off a train
hook_candidates.why: Achievement and vanishing collide in one line, the Flight 19 shape.

hook_candidates.text: Cinema's real inventor disappeared weeks before he could prove it
hook_candidates.why: Strong, but 'real inventor' asks the viewer to take a side first.

hook_candidates.text: A man boarded at Dijon and never got off
hook_candidates.why: Good loop, but without the achievement it is just a missing person.

hook_choice.reason: The collision is the story: the man who did it first is also the man who disappeared, and both halves land in eleven words.

factual_claims.text: Louis Le Prince filmed Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds on 14 October 1888 using his single-lens camera.
Le Prince vanished on 16 September 1890 after saying goodbye to his brother at Dijon and boarding a train for Paris, and never arrived.
Neither Le Prince's body nor his luggage was ever recovered, and a public exhibition of his films was planned at the Morris-Jumel Mansion in Manhattan for September 1890.
Theories for his disappearance include suicide over financial difficulties, murder linked to the motion-picture patent disputes involving Edison, and a voluntary disappearance.
A photograph of a drowned man resembling Le Prince was found in Paris police archives, and Le Prince was declared dead in absentia on 16 September 1897.

segments.narration: He shot the first moving picture, then vanished off a train. Louis Le Prince. October 1888, Leeds — seconds of his family walking in a garden.
The 16th of September, 1890. He says goodbye to his brother at Dijon and boards the express for Paris. He never gets off it.
No body. No luggage. Nothing recovered, then or since. And a public showing of his films was already booked in Manhattan.
The theories piled up. Suicide over money. Murder over the patents, with Edison's camp the suspect. A family quarrel. A simple robbery.
A photograph of a drowned man resembling him later surfaced in Paris police files. It is the closest anyone has come. He was declared dead in absentia in 1897.

research.summary: Louis Le Prince, a French-American inventor, filmed Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds on 14 October 1888. He vanished on 16 September 1890 after boarding a Dijon-Paris train; neither he nor his luggage was ever found, and a Manhattan exhibition of his films was planned for that month. Theories include suicide over money, murder tied to the patent disputes involving Edison, and voluntary disappearance; none is conclusive. A photograph of a drowning victim resembling him was found in Paris police archives. He was declared dead in absentia in 1897. The narration does not date the photograph's discovery, as the two sources differ (1903 archives vs surfacing in 2003).

At its height Villa Epecuén could accommodate at least 5,000 visitors, drawn by the lake's very high salinity.
In November 1985 a seiche caused by a rare weather pattern broke a nearby dam and then the dike protecting the village.

segments.narration: This spa town spent twenty-five years under ten metres of water. Villa Epecuén sat on a salt lake in Argentina, and it was packed.
At its peak it hosted five thousand visitors at once, drawn by water saltier than the sea. Then November nineteen eighty-five arrived.
A rare weather pattern shoved the whole lake sideways. The seiche broke the dam, then the dike. How do you outrun a lake?
The water did not drain. It kept rising until ten metres covered the rooftops, and it stayed for twenty-five years.
In two thousand nine the lake receded and Epecuén reappeared, bleached white, trees like bone. One man moved back. Pablo Novak lived there alone until he died in twenty twenty-four.

research.summary: Villa Epecuén was a salt-lake spa resort in Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, developed from the 1920s and at its height able to host at least 5,000 visitors. In November 1985 a seiche driven by a rare weather pattern broke a dam and then the dike protecting the town, and water eventually stood about 10 metres deep over it. The lake receded from 2009, exposing salt-bleached ruins; Pablo Novak returned that year as the only resident and lived there until his death on 22 January 2024, after which the village was declared deserted.

stories.title: Three Girls Started Laughing In 1962. It Closed 14 Schools.
stories.description: In January 1962 three pupils at a girls' school in Kashasha, Tanganyika started laughing and could not stop. The fits spread to about a thousand people and shut fourteen schools before doctors worked out what was actually happening. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #1962
stories.editorial_rationale: Skyquake (hook 138.1%) and Mirage of Constanz (187.7%) are the brief's two best hooks and both state something ordinary people experienced, flat and cold, so this opens on the three girls rather than on Tanganyika's independence context.

hook_candidates.why: The strangest physical detail, stated flat, with the cause withheld.

hook_candidates.text: A laughing fit closed fourteen schools in nineteen sixty-two.
hook_candidates.why: Leads on scale, but 'laughing fit' sounds figurative before the detail lands.

hook_candidates.why: Strong numbers, but the ratio needs a school explained first.

factual_claims.text: The outbreak began on 30 January 1962 at a mission-run girls' boarding school in Kashasha, Tanganyika, starting with three pupils.
95 of the school's 159 pupils were affected, with symptoms lasting from a few hours to 16 days.
Investigating medical officers found no infectious or toxic cause for the episodes.
The school closed in March 1962, the outbreak reached Nshamba village and other communities, and about 1,000 people were affected across 14 closed schools.
Medical officers A. M. Rankin and P. J. Philip published their investigation in the Central African Journal of Medicine in 1963, diagnosing mass psychogenic illness.

segments.narration: Three schoolgirls started laughing and couldn't stop for days. Kashasha, Tanganyika, the thirtieth of January, nineteen sixty-two.
It spread. Ninety-five of the school's one hundred fifty-nine pupils were affected, in fits that ran from hours to sixteen days.
Doctors found nothing. No fever, no toxin, no poisoned food. So what travels through a school and leaves no trace in the blood?
The school closed in March. The laughter went home with the girls, reached Nshamba village, and eventually touched about a thousand people across fourteen schools.
Medical officers Rankin and Philip published the answer in nineteen sixty-three: mass psychogenic illness. Real symptoms, no pathogen, stress moving through a community like weather.

research.summary: The Tanganyika laughter epidemic began on 30 January 1962 at a mission-run girls' boarding school in Kashasha, near Bukoba on the western shore of Lake Victoria. It started with three girls and affected 95 of the school's 159 pupils, aged 12 to 18, with episodes lasting from a few hours to 16 days. The school closed on 18 March 1962; the outbreak spread to Nshamba and other communities within about a 100-mile radius of Bukoba, closing 14 schools and affecting roughly 1,000 people over some 18 months. Medical officers A. M. Rankin and P. J. Philip investigated and published in the Central African Journal of Medicine in 1963, concluding it was mass psychogenic illness — real symptoms with no infectious or toxic cause, later analysed by Bartholomew, Wessely and Hempelmann as conversion reactions under cultural and academic stress in a newly independent country.

stories.title: Paper Won't Fit Between These 100-Ton Inca Stones
stories.description: The terrace walls above Cusco are built from limestone blocks weighing over a hundred tonnes, cut to fit each other exactly and laid without a gram of mortar. Here is what the chroniclers and the archaeology actually say about how it was done. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #inca
stories.editorial_rationale: Mirage of Constanz holds the brief's best hook at 187.7% by stating one impossible-sounding image cold, so this opens on the paper-and-hundred-tonne contrast instead of the place-and-date framing that left Anglo-Zanzibar at 51.5%.

hook_candidates.why: A big number, but weight alone is easy to shrug off.

hook_candidates.text: A sheet of paper won't fit between these hundred-ton stones.
hook_candidates.why: Two scales in one image, the tiniest and the heaviest, which is what makes it feel impossible.

hook_candidates.text: Spaniards spent centuries stealing this wall and left the big stones.
hook_candidates.why: Good on the aftermath, but needs the wall introduced first.

factual_claims.text: Sacsayhuamán's largest limestone blocks weigh from about 128 to nearly 200 tonnes and are fitted without mortar so tightly that a coin or paper will not pass between them.
The three main terrace walls run roughly 400 metres long, built from irregular blocks laid without mortar.
The stone was brought from quarries kilometres away, and the Inca had no iron tools, wheeled vehicles or draft animals.
Pedro Cieza de León recorded in 1553 that Pachacuti assigned 20,000 workers, with 4,000 quarrying stone and 6,000 hauling it on leather cables.
Inca blocks show hammerstone impact marks and were fitted by repeated adjustment, and the mortarless inclined masonry gives the walls exceptional seismic resistance.

segments.narration: A sheet of paper won't fit between these hundred-ton stones. Sacsayhuamán, above Cusco, at three thousand seven hundred metres.
No mortar. Every block a different shape, and every one meets its neighbours exactly. Three terraced walls, each about four hundred metres long.
The limestone came from quarries kilometres away, over Andean ridges, with no iron tools, no wheels and no draft animals. So how?
Cieza de León wrote in fifteen fifty-three that Pachacuti put twenty thousand men on it, four thousand quarrying, six thousand hauling on leather cables.

Best reconstruction: pounded to shape with hammerstones, hauled on ropes and ramps, test-fitted again and again. And the crooked joints are the point. Inca walls settle back into place when the ground shakes.

research.summary: Sacsayhuamán is an Inca walled complex on the northern edge of Cusco, Peru, at 3,701 m. Its three main terrace walls run about 400 m and are built of limestone blocks of roughly 128 to nearly 200 tonnes, fitted without mortar; Pedro Cieza de León wrote in 1553 that 'a rial could not be put in between two of them' and that Pachacuti set 20,000 workers on the site, 4,000 quarrying and 6,000 hauling with leather cables. After the conquest the finer masonry was quarried for colonial Cusco, leaving the largest blocks. Wikipedia's Inca architecture article records that stones were initially fitted using hammerstones, whose impact marks survive on many faces, that blocks were lifted with rope slings and adjusted by eye, and that inclined walls with rounded corners and thorough masonry gave Inca buildings 'peerless seismic resistance', with blocks observed settling back into position after strong earthquakes.

stories.title: New York Read About Moon Bat-People And Believed It
stories.description: In August 1835 the New York Sun ran six articles describing bison, unicorns and winged man-bats living on the moon, all credited to a real astronomer who knew nothing about it. Yale sent scientists to check. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #1835
stories.editorial_rationale: Desert shipwrecks sat at 68.9% hook hold because it opened on legend rather than record, so this one leads with the documented fact that a newspaper printed it as news, in the flat cold-statement shape that put Mirage of Constanz at 187.7%.

hook_candidates.text: A New York paper reported bat-winged people living on the moon.
hook_candidates.why: The strangest concrete detail, presented as something that was actually printed.

hook_candidates.text: In eighteen thirty-five, readers believed the moon had unicorns.
hook_candidates.why: Opens on the date, which the brief's weaker hooks all do.

factual_claims.text: In August 1835 the New York Sun published articles reporting bat-winged humanoids living on the moon.
The six articles described lunar bison, single-horned goats, beaches and temples, plus 'Vespertilio-homo' man-bats that walked upright and flew.
The discoveries were falsely credited to the real astronomer Sir John Herschel, who was observing at the Cape of Good Hope and had no involvement.
A committee of Yale scientists travelled to New York to find the original Edinburgh journal articles, which did not exist.
Sun reporter Richard Adams Locke wrote the series as satire, and The Sun admitted the articles were fabricated on 16 September 1835 without printing a retraction.

segments.narration: A New York paper reported bat-winged people living on the moon. The Sun ran it as news in August eighteen thirty-five.
Six articles. Lunar bison, goats with a single horn, beaches, temples, and Vespertilio-homo, man-bats who walked upright and flew.
It was all credited to Sir John Herschel, a real astronomer, genuinely observing at the Cape of Good Hope. He knew nothing about it.
New York believed it. A committee of Yale scientists came down to read the original journal articles. There were none. Who writes this, and why?
Richard Adams Locke, a Sun reporter, wrote it as satire of serious claims that the moon was populated. The Sun admitted the fabrication on the sixteenth of September and never printed a retraction.

research.summary: The Great Moon Hoax was a series of six articles in the New York Sun beginning 25 August 1835, purporting to report Sir John Herschel's discovery of life on the moon through a vast new telescope at the Cape of Good Hope. The articles described lunar bison, single-horned goats, tail-less beavers, beaches and temples, and winged humanoids named Vespertilio-homo, or man-bats. They were attributed to Herschel via a fictitious companion, Dr Andrew Grant; Herschel, who really was observing at the Cape, had nothing to do with them. Readers took them as fact, and a committee of Yale scientists travelled to New York looking for the non-existent Edinburgh Journal of Science originals. Sun reporter Richard Adams Locke, who publicly admitted authorship in 1840, is accepted as the author and is understood to have written the pieces as satire of contemporary speculation about extraterrestrial life. The Sun acknowledged the articles were fabricated on 16 September 1835 but issued no formal retraction.

stories.title: Nobody Could Dig Up Laos's 2,000 Stone Jars For Decades
stories.description: More than two thousand carved stone jars stand across a plateau in Laos, some six tonnes each, and for decades archaeologists could not safely reach them. What was keeping them out was dropped there in the twentieth century. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #archaeology
stories.editorial_rationale: SS Huronian held 107.2% by opening on something that should not be possible, so this hook leads with the fact that a whole archaeological landscape was off-limits and saves the reason, matching that shape rather than a date-first opener.

hook_candidates.text: A field of giant stone jars nobody could safely excavate.
hook_candidates.why: Two mysteries in one line, the jars and the reason they were untouchable.

hook_candidates.text: Two thousand stone jars sit across a plateau in Laos.
hook_candidates.why: Clean and factual, but it asks nothing of the viewer.

hook_candidates.text: Some of these stone jars weigh six tons and hold bones.
hook_candidates.why: Gives away the burial answer far too early.

hook_choice.reason: It opens a loop the other two close, and 'safely' is the word that makes a viewer need the next line.

factual_claims.text: More than 2,100 megalithic stone jars stand across more than 120 recorded sites on the Xiangkhoang Plateau in Laos.
The jars range from about 1 to 3 metres in height and weigh up to about six tonnes, carved from stone.
An estimated 270 million cluster bombs were dropped or dumped on the Plain of Jars and about 80 million failed to detonate, restricting archaeological access.
Clearance operations from 2004 opened sites for study, and optically stimulated luminescence dating placed jars in position as early as about 1240 BC.
Excavations found human remains, beads and iron tools with the jars, and UNESCO inscribed them in 2019 as Iron Age funerary vessels.

segments.narration: A field of giant stone jars nobody could safely excavate. More than two thousand of them, across the Xiangkhoang Plateau in Laos.
Up to three metres tall, six tonnes each, carved from solid rock. Nobody living remembers putting them there.
And archaeologists mostly couldn't get near them. Around two hundred and seventy million cluster bombs were dropped on this plateau. Roughly eighty million never went off.
Clearance work from two thousand four opened the sites. Optical dating put the jars in place as early as around twelve forty BC.
Inside and around them: human bone, beads, iron tools. They are funerary vessels, a plateau-sized graveyard, and what kept it a mystery was a war three thousand years too late.

research.summary: The Plain of Jars is a megalithic landscape on the Xiangkhoang Plateau in Laos, with more than 2,100 carved stone jars recorded across more than 120 sites. The jars stand roughly 1 to 3 metres tall and weigh up to about six tonnes, with the largest site holding several hundred. Optically stimulated luminescence dating places jars in position as early as 1240 to 660 BC, and excavations from Madeleine Colani onward have recovered human remains, glass beads, spindle whorls and bronze and iron tools, supporting the accepted reading of the jars as Iron Age funerary vessels used for secondary burial. An estimated 270 million cluster bombs were dropped or dumped on the plateau, of which around 80 million failed to detonate, which severely restricted archaeological access until clearance operations began in 2004. UNESCO inscribed the Megalithic Jar Sites in Xiengkhuang on the World Heritage List in 2019.

segments.narration: Henry Ford built an American town in the Amazon rainforest. Nineteen twenty-eight, on the Tapajos River in Brazil. He called it Fordlandia.
About two and a half million acres, all for rubber. Clapboard houses, a water tower, hamburgers, square dances, and no alcohol.
Workers rioted in nineteen thirty over the canteen food. But the thing that actually killed Fordlandia was not the people.
Rubber trees grow wild and scattered in the Amazon for a reason. Planted in tight rows, they hand South American leaf blight one continuous meal.
The blight took it. Belterra, downstream, died the same way. In nineteen forty-five Ford's grandson sold both back to Brazil at a loss above twenty million dollars, and Henry Ford never once visited.

research.summary: Fordlandia was founded in 1928 by Henry Ford on the east bank of the Tapajos River, about 300 km south of Santarem in Para, Brazil, on a concession of roughly 2.5 million acres, as a rubber plantation and prefabricated American-style town intended for 10,000 residents. American housing, diet and social rules, including prohibition of alcohol, provoked the 1930 'Breaking Pans' (Quebra-Panelas) revolt. The plantation failed biologically: Hevea rubber planted densely in its native range is highly vulnerable to South American leaf blight, along with ants, lace bugs and caterpillars, in a way that scattered wild trees and the transplanted Asian plantations were not. Fordlandia was abandoned in 1934 and operations moved downstream to Belterra, which also failed. In 1945 Henry Ford II sold both sites back to Brazil at a loss exceeding $20 million. Henry Ford never visited either site; most of the original structures still stand and the area had around 3,000 residents as of 2017.

segments.narration: An airliner vanished four minutes from its runway. August 1947, a converted Lancaster bomber crossing the Andes to Santiago.
Its last Morse message ended in one word nobody could decode: STENDEC. Sent three times, fast and clean.
Eleven people gone. Searchers combed the mountains for weeks and found nothing at all. How does a plane disappear on a route it flew every week?
Fifty-one years later, climbers on Mount Tupungato found a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine melting out of a glacier.

The crew had flown into the jet stream, barely understood in 1947. A fierce headwind held them back, so they descended thinking the peaks were behind them. The mountain kept them until the ice let go.

research.summary: On 2 August 1947 the Avro Lancastrian G-AGWH, RMA Star Dust, flew from Buenos Aires to Santiago with 11 aboard and disappeared after a Morse message timed at 17:41 giving an ETA of 17:45 and ending 'STENDEC'. No trace was found until 1998, when Argentine climbers found a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine emerging from a glacier on Mount Tupungato at about 15,000 feet; further wreckage was recovered in 2000. The accepted reconstruction is controlled flight into terrain: the crew, crossing at 24,000 feet, met the jet stream, whose strong headwind was not understood in 1947, over-estimated their ground speed and began descent while still behind cloud-covered peaks. STENDEC itself remains unexplained.

segments.narration: A healthy man could be dead by supper. England, 1485, and a new sickness was moving faster than any plague.
It started with shivering, then a drenching sweat. Survivors recovered in a day. Many never got the day.
It struck the young and strong hardest. Two teenage brothers, dukes of Suffolk, died within an hour of each other. Why would a disease pick the healthy?
Five epidemics came and went across seventy years. After 1551 it never returned anywhere, ever again.

The leading modern answer is a hantavirus carried by rodents, argued in a 2014 study from the disease's speed and incubation pattern. No sample of it survives to test, so the sweat keeps both its name and its secret.

research.summary: The English sweating sickness appeared in England in August 1485 and returned in roughly five epidemics, the last in 1551, which began in Shrewsbury in April. Onset was abrupt — cold shivers, dizziness, headache, severe neck and shoulder pain — followed by profuse sweating, racing pulse and collapse, with death or recovery typically inside 8 to 24 hours. It notably killed young, well-fed adults: Henry Brandon, 2nd Duke of Suffolk (15), and his brother Charles (13) died in 1551 about an hour apart, and two lord mayors, six aldermen and three sheriffs died in London in 1485. After 1551 it was never recorded again. Heyman, Simons and Cochez argued in the journal Viruses in 2014 that an unknown Old World hantavirus fits the symptom picture and incubation window; anthrax (McSweegan, 2004), relapsing fever, ergotism and influenza have been considered and largely set aside. No pathogen sample exists, so no hypothesis has been confirmed.

segments.narration: These scrolls turn to dust if you open them. Vesuvius carbonised an entire Roman library in 79 AD.
Workmen found them under Herculaneum in 1752. Over eighteen hundred blackened rolls, hard as coal.
Scholars sliced them open. Scraped them. Unrolled them over four years each. Most were destroyed to read a few lines. What do you do with a book that dies when you look at it?
Answer: don't open it. Researchers X-ray scanned the sealed rolls and trained software to spot ink invisible to the eye.
In 2023 a student pulled one word out of a scroll nobody had opened: porphyras, purple. By 2026 a whole scroll had been read end to end, a Stoic treatise sealed since the eruption.

research.summary: The Herculaneum papyri are the only library to survive from classical antiquity, carbonised rather than burnt when pyroclastic flows from Vesuvius buried Herculaneum in AD 79 in a low-oxygen environment. Workmen found the Villa of the Papyri in 1752; the official inventory lists 1,814 rolls and fragments, of which roughly 340 are near complete. Early reading methods were destructive: Camillo Paderni sliced scrolls lengthwise to transcribe them, and Antonio Piaggio's mechanical unroller, begun in 1756, took about four years per scroll and exposed ink that faded in air. The Vesuvius Challenge, launched in March 2023, applied X-ray phase-contrast tomography and machine learning to sealed scrolls. In October 2023 the first word, 'porphyras', was recovered; in February 2024 the grand prize team revealed about 5% of one scroll, Philodemus on music and food; and in 2026 PHerc. 1667 became the first scroll virtually unwrapped and read end to end, giving 22 columns of a Stoic treatise.

segments.narration: A star dropped twenty-two percent of its light. Then brightened. Then dipped again, on no schedule at all.
Volunteers sifting Kepler telescope data flagged it in 2015. About fifteen hundred light years away, in Cygnus.

A planet blocks maybe one percent. This was twenty-two. Something enormous and ragged was crossing the star, and nobody could name it. So astronomers said the quiet part out loud: alien megastructure.
The test was colour. A solid object blocks every wavelength equally. Dust does not.
The star dimmed more in ultraviolet than in infrared. Whatever crosses it is fine dust, not a swarm of panels. The most famous alien signal of the decade turned out to be a cloud of grit.

research.summary: KIC 8462852, known as Tabby's Star or Boyajian's Star, lies about 1,470 light-years away in Cygnus. Citizen scientists on the Planet Hunters project spotted irregular, aperiodic dips in its Kepler light curve, reaching up to about 22 percent — far deeper than any transiting planet — and the result was published in a 2015 paper led by Tabetha Boyajian. Because no natural cause fitted, Jason Wright and others floated a Dyson swarm as a speculative option, which drove the 'alien megastructure' coverage. A crowdfunded Las Cumbres Observatory campaign then watched fresh dips across wavelengths: the January 2018 study found the dimming is stronger in ultraviolet than in infrared. An opaque solid would dim all wavelengths equally, so the wavelength dependence rules a solid structure out and points to fine circumstellar dust. Lead author Huan Meng stated this 'pretty much rules out the alien megastructure theory'.

factual_claims.text: The Baigong pipes are on and near Mount Baigong, about 40 kilometres southwest of Delingha in Qinghai Province, China.
They are found in three caves in the mountain and along the shore of a nearby salt lake, and reach up to about 40 centimetres in diameter.

segments.narration: Iron pipes run through solid rock in a Chinese desert. Mount Baigong, Qinghai, forty kilometres from the nearest town.
They sit in three caves and along the shore of a salt lake. Some are forty centimetres across, rust-red, going straight into the cliff.
Nobody lived here. No smelter, no settlement, no road. By 2002 newspapers were calling it an alien refuelling station, and one report claimed the pipes were radioactive.
Then geologists cut them open and found tree rings.

They are casts of tree roots. Iron-rich sediment filled the channels the roots left behind, the wood rotted away, and the mineral shell hardened into a pipe. The desert did not build them. It grew them.

research.summary: The Baigong pipes are rust-coloured, tube-shaped formations on and near Mount Baigong, about 40 km southwest of Delingha in Qinghai Province, China, found in three caves and along the shore of Toson Lake. They range up to about 40 cm in diameter. A June 2002 report in the Henan Dahe Bao, followed by local officials speaking to journalists on 16 June 2002, made them internationally famous as an 'alien refuelling station', and a 2007 investigation claimed some were highly radioactive. Chinese scientists analysing them by atomic emission spectroscopy found roughly 30% iron oxide with silicon dioxide and calcium oxide, plus organic plant matter and what looked like tree rings. A 2003 Xinmin Weekly report gave the explanation scientists found most likely: the pipes are fossilised casts of tree roots. Under the right temperature and chemical conditions, iron-rich sediment filled and replaced the root channels while the wood decayed, leaving a hollow mineral tube. The Qaidam Basin was warm and well vegetated in prehistory, which fits.

stories.title: Archaeologists Found This Tomb In 1974 And Never Opened It
stories.description: Farmers digging a well in 1974 hit the edge of the first Chinese emperor's burial complex, and the terracotta army was only the outer guard. The tomb itself is still sealed, and the soil above it is loaded with mercury. #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory #china
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's top hook cohort rewards a short, physical opening line (Dyatlov Pass, 89.3% hook hold, eight words), so the hook here is the mercury in the soil rather than the emperor's name or the terracotta army everyone already knows.

factual_claims.text: The mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang stands in Lintong District, Xi'an, Shaanxi, under a burial mound about 76 metres tall, and soil surveys there found anomalously high mercury.
Farmers digging a well found terracotta warrior fragments in March 1974, and excavation revealed about 7,000 terracotta figures in battle formation.

Sima Qian, writing roughly a century after the burial, described mercury made to simulate the hundred rivers, the Yangtze, the Yellow River and the sea, set to flow mechanically, beneath a representation of the heavens.
Soil surveys measured mercury far above the regional background over the tomb mound, with the highest readings clustered in a pattern resembling the geography of China's rivers.
The central tomb chamber has never been excavated on preservation grounds, including the rapid deterioration of pigment on terracotta figures once exposed in 1974.

segments.narration: The soil above this grave is thick with mercury. Lintong, near Xi'an, under a hill seventy-six metres tall.
Farmers digging a well in 1974 hit its outer edge. Thousands of terracotta soldiers, standing in battle formation.
Those were the guards. The tomb itself has never been opened. A historian writing a century later said it held a hundred rivers of mercury, flowing mechanically, under a ceiling of stars.
For centuries that read as legend. Then surveys measured the soil: mercury far above the regional background, clustered where China's real rivers would sit on a map.
So archaeologists stopped. Terracotta paint flaked away within minutes of exposure in 1974, and nobody can promise better today. The rivers stay sealed until technology catches up.

research.summary: Qin Shi Huang's mausoleum sits in Lintong District, Xi'an, Shaanxi. Work began in 246 BCE when he took the throne at thirteen and continued for roughly 38 years; the truncated-pyramid burial mound stands about 76 metres tall over an underground palace measured at roughly 80 by 50 metres. Farmers digging a well found terracotta fragments in March 1974; formal excavation from May 1974 uncovered three pits holding about 7,000 terracotta warriors and horses. These are the outer complex — the central tomb chamber has never been opened. The historian Sima Qian, writing about a century after the burial, described mercury simulating the hundred rivers, the Yangtze, the Yellow River and the sea, set to flow mechanically under a modelled heaven. Soil surveys since the 1980s found mercury far above the regional background over the mound — Wikipedia cites an average around 205 ppb with one point at 1,440 ppb; other summaries of the same survey work give about 250 ppb average against roughly 30 ppb regionally, peaking near 1,500 ppb — with the highest readings clustered in a pattern echoing China's real river geography. Excavation is held back by preservation concerns, most concretely the pigment that flaked off terracotta figures within minutes of exposure in 1974.
